items.title: Derivative rules for differentiable matrix-valued curves, and skewness of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ for a curve in $SO(3)$
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $t_0\in I$ and let $A,B:I\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be **differentiable at $t_0$**, meaning ([[def-matrix-space]]) that every entry function $t\mapsto A(t)_{ij}$ and $t\mapsto B(t)_{ij}$ is differentiable at $t_0$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]]; write $A'(t_0)$ for the matrix with entries $A'(t_0)_{ij}:=(t\mapsto A(t)_{ij})'(t_0)$, and similarly for $B$.

1. $A+B$ and $A^{\mathsf T}$ are differentiable at $t_0$, with $(A+B)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)+B'(t_0)$ and $(A^{\mathsf T})'(t_0)=(A'(t_0))^{\mathsf T}$.
2. $AB$ is differentiable at $t_0$, with $(AB)'(t_0)=A'(t_0)B(t_0)+A(t_0)B'(t_0)$.
3. If $A(t)\in SO(3)$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), then the matrix $A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}A'(t_0)$ is skew-symmetric, i.e. $(A^{\mathsf T}A')^{\mathsf T}=-A^{\mathsf T}A'$ at $t_0$, and likewise $A'(t_0)A(t_0)^{\mathsf T}$ is skew-symmetric. In particular the trace of each of these two matrices vanishes.

items.title: The skew-matrix/cross-product correspondence $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ and its conjugation law $R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times$
items.statement:
Use the standard basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ and coordinates $\omega=\omega_1e_1+\omega_2e_2+\omega_3e_3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Define the map $[\cdot]_\times:\mathbb R^3\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ by
$$[\omega]_\times:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\ \omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\ -\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then:

1. $[\omega]_\times z=\omega\times z$ for all $\omega,z\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
2. $[\omega]_\times^{\mathsf T}=-[\omega]_\times$ for every $\omega$; the map $\omega\mapsto[\omega]_\times$ is linear and injective, and its image is exactly the set of skew-symmetric matrices of $M_3(\mathbb R)$. Consequently every skew-symmetric $\Omega\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ equals $[\omega]_\times$ for exactly one $\omega$, namely $\omega=(\Omega_{32},\Omega_{13},\Omega_{21})$.
3. For every $R\in SO(3)$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) and every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$R[\omega]_\times R^{\mathsf T}=[R\omega]_\times.$$

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.1.1, Eqs. (3.5)-(3.7), printed pp. 47-48: the antisymmetric angular-velocity matrix and its single-index vector

items.title: Mass distributions on $\mathbb R^3$: total mass, first moment and inertia matrix
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) and let $
u$ be a measure on the measurable space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-measure-space]]) that is **finite**, $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$, and **bounded**, meaning that there is a real $R>0$ with
$$
u igl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0) igr)=0,$$
the closed ball being that of [[def-metric-ball]]. Throughout, integrals are Lebesgue integrals against $
u$ in the sense of [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], and for a measurable vector- or matrix-valued function the integral is defined **componentwise**: $\int F\,d
u:= igl(\int F_1\,d
u,\int F_2\,d
u,\int F_3\,d
u igr)$ and $ igl(\int M\,d
u igr)_{jk}:=\int M_{jk}\,d
u$, whenever every displayed scalar integral is finite.

A **mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$** is a bounded finite Borel measure $
u$ with $m:=
u(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$; the number $m$ is its **total mass**. Writing points of $\mathbb R^3$ as $ho$ and using the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdotangle$ and norm $\lVerthoVert_2=\sqrt{\langleho,hoangle}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define:

1. the **first moment** $\mu(
u):=\intho\,d
u\in\mathbb R^3$, read componentwise as $\mu(
u)_j=\intho_j\,d
u$;
2. the **inertia matrix** $I(
u)\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) by its entries $I(
u)_{jk}:=\int igl(\lVerthoVert_2^2\,\delta_{jk}-ho_jho_k igr)\,d
u$, where $\delta_{jk}=1$ if $j=k$ and $\delta_{jk}=0$ otherwise; equivalently $I(
u)=\int igl(\lVerthoVert_2^2 I_3-hoho^{\mathsf T} igr)\,d
u$ with $I_3$ the identity matrix and $hoho^{\mathsf T}$ the matrix product of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

The mass distribution is **centred** when $\mu(
u)=0$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), each of the integrals above is a finite real number: on $\overline B_R(0)$ one has $|ho_j|\le R$ and $|ho_jho_k|\le R^2$, and $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$; the precise statement and proof are [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]], which depends on this definition only for its notation. The assumption is used there exactly once, to obtain the Borel measurability of the polynomial integrands from the published continuity criterion; every later item that invokes this finiteness carries the assumption explicitly.

items.title: Finiteness of the moments of a bounded finite Borel measure on $\mathbb R^3$
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $
u$ be a measure on $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]) that is finite and bounded: $
u(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0))=0$ for some $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). Then:

1. for all $j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$ the functions $ho\mapstoho_j$ and $ho\mapstoho_jho_k$ are Borel measurable and $
u$-integrable, with $\int\lvertho_jvert\,d
u\le R\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$ and $\int\lvertho_jho_kvert\,d
u\le R^2\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$;
2. consequently the total mass $m=
u(\mathbb R^3)$, the first moment $\mu(
u)$ and every entry of the inertia matrix $I(
u)$ of the definition are well-defined finite real numbers, and $\lvert\mu(
u)_jvert\le R\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$ while $\lvert I(
u)_{jk}vert\le 2R^2\,
u(\mathbb R^3)$.

items.title: Rigid placements, body and spatial angular velocity, and material velocities
items.statement:
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $\nu$ be a mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ with total mass $m$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]), let $c:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable and let $R:I\to SO(3)$ be differentiable ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), differentiability meaning entrywise differentiability of $R$ in the sense of [[def-derivative]] with derivative $R'$; write $c'$ for the derivative of $c$.

The **rigid placement with reference shape $\nu$, translation $c$ and rotation $R$** is the map
$$x:I\times\mathbb R^3\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad x(t,\rho):=c(t)+R(t)\rho,$$
so that the material point labelled by $\rho$ (a point of the reference shape) is carried to $x(t,\rho)$ at time $t$; the map $x(t,\cdot)$ is the **placement at time $t$**, and the pair $(c(t),R(t))$ is its **configuration**. The **material velocity** of the label $\rho$ at time $t$ is the derivative
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho):=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho,$$
which exists by differentiability of $c$ and of the entries of $R$.

**Body and spatial angular velocity.** By [[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] the matrix $R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I$. By [[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] there is therefore a unique vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times,$$
and the map $\omega:I\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the placement; the **spatial angular velocity** is $\omega_{\mathrm{s}}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)$. Explicitly $\omega(t)=\bigl((R^{\mathsf T}R')_{32},(R^{\mathsf T}R')_{13},(R^{\mathsf T}R')_{21}\bigr)(t)$, a finite linear expression in the entries of $R$ and $R'$; consequently, if $R$ is twice differentiable, then $\omega$ is differentiable and its derivative is the **body angular acceleration**.

Equivalently, by the conjugation clause of [[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], $R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm{s}}(t)]_\times$.

items.title: Symmetry, the quadratic identity $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^2\,d\nu$, and the positive-definiteness criterion for the inertia matrix
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only in [L1], through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]], to make the entries of $I$ finite real numbers. Let $
u$ be a mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ with total mass $m=
u(\mathbb R^3)$ and inertia matrix $I=I(
u)$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]). Write $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega:=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\omega_jI_{jk}\omega_k$ for the quadratic form of $I$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lVert\cdotVert_2$ for the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $I$ is symmetric: $I_{jk}=I_{kj}$ for all $j,k$.
2. For every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega	imeshoVert_2^2\,d
u(ho)\ \ge 0,$$ the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
3. The symmetric bilinear form $(u,v)\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}Iv$ on $\mathbb R^3$ is therefore positive semidefinite ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); for each $\omega
e0$, writing $\mathbb R\omega=\{t\omega:t\in\mathbb R\}$, one has $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=0$ if and only if $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega)=0$. Thus it is positive definite if and only if $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega)>0$ for every $\omega
e0$, that is, no line through the origin carries the entire mass ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
4. If the form is positive definite, then $I$ is invertible.

items.title: Principal axes and principal moments of the inertia matrix, and positivity in the nondegenerate case
items.statement:
Let $
u$ be a mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ with inertia matrix $I=I(
u)$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]), and write $I\omega$ for the matrix-vector product and $\langle\cdot,\cdotangle$ for the Euclidean inner product on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. there is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-orthogonal-vectors-sets-and-orthonormal-bases]]) and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$ with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ for $j=1,2,3$;
2. for any such basis and any $\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j$ one has $I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$, $I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j$, and $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^2=\int\lVert\omega	imeshoVert_2^2\,d
u(ho)\ \ge0$;
3. each $I_j$ vanishes exactly when $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j)=0$, that is, the whole mass lies on the line $\mathbb Re_j$; if the inertia form is positive definite then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible with $I^{-1}e_j=I_j^{-1}e_j$; and if $
u$ is not supported on any line through the origin, meaning that $
u(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega)>0$ for every $\omega
e0$, then every $I_j>0$.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.2, the diagonalization discussion after Eq. (3.20), printed pp. 50-52: principal axes and principal moments via orthogonal diagonalization of the symmetric inertia tensor

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §2.5 (Principal Moments of Inertia): the eigensystem of the inertia tensor and the diagonal form
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.3: principal axes of the inertia tensor and their positivity

items.title: Euler's equations $I\omega'+\omega\times I\omega=R^{\mathsf T}\tau$ under an adopted torque balance, and the torque-free invariants and principal-axis equations
items.statement:
Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $\nu$ be a centred mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ that is not supported on any line through the origin, with inertia matrix $I$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]), let $c:J\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable and let $R:J\to SO(3)$ be twice differentiable, and let $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ be the rigid placement with body angular velocity $\omega$ ([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]). Write $l:=I\omega:J\to\mathbb R^3$; by [[cor-cm-principal-axes-of-the-inertia-matrix]] the inertia form is positive definite and $I$ is invertible.

Adopt the **balance hypothesis** (B): there is a map $\tau:J\to\mathbb R^3$ such that the curve $t\mapsto R(t)l(t)$ is differentiable and
$$(Rl)'(t)=\tau(t)\qquad(t\in J).$$
Then:

1. $l$ is differentiable and **Euler's equations with torque** hold: $$I\omega'+\omega\times I\omega=R^{\mathsf T}\tau\qquad\text{on }J;$$
2. if $\tau=0$ on $J$, then $l$ satisfies the **torque-free Euler equations** $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$, and the functions $t\mapsto\langle l(t),l(t)\rangle$ and $t\mapsto\tfrac12\langle l(t),I^{-1}l(t)\rangle=\tfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$ are constant on $J$;
3. if $\tau=0$ on $J$ and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is a positively oriented orthonormal eigenbasis of $I$ with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ and $l=\sum_jl_je_j$, then $\langle l,l\rangle=\sum_jl_j^2$ and $\tfrac12\langle l,I^{-1}l\rangle=\sum_jl_j^2/(2I_j)$ are constant on $J$, and the torque-free equations read $$l_1'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_3}-\frac1{I_2}\Bigr)l_2l_3,\qquad l_2'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_1}-\frac1{I_3}\Bigr)l_1l_3,\qquad l_3'=\Bigl(\frac1{I_2}-\frac1{I_1}\Bigr)l_1l_2.$$

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.3, Eqs. (3.31)-(3.33), printed pp. 53-55: angular-momentum rate, Euler's equations in the principal body frame and the torque extension
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.4, Eq. (4.66): Euler equations $I_j\dot\omega_j+(I_{j''}-I_{j'})\omega_{j'}\omega_{j''}=\tau_j$

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §2.9 (Euler's Equations), Eqs. (2.80)-(2.83): angular-momentum evolution and Euler equations in principal components

items.title: Lyapunov stability of spin about the largest and smallest principal axes of the torque-free top
items.statement:
Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$ be positive reals and let $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear map with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ on the standard orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$. Consider the autonomous first-order system
$$l'(t)=F(l(t)),\qquad F(l):=l\times(I^{-1}l),$$
on $U:=\mathbb R^3$, read as in [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]] with the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and $I^{-1}$ the inverse of $I$ ([[cor-cm-principal-axes-of-the-inertia-matrix]]); this is the torque-free Euler system of [[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]] in angular-momentum variables. Let $L\ne0$. Then:

$Le_1$ and $Le_3$ are equilibria of $F$ and each is Lyapunov stable in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]: for $j=1$ and $j=3$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $l$ with $\lVert l(0)-Le_j\rVert_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\lVert l(t)-Le_j\rVert_2<\varepsilon$ for every $t\ge0$.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §§3.5.1-3.4.3, Eqs. (3.34)-(3.45), printed pp. 55-58: free symmetric top, and the asymmetric-top stability discussion with the invariants of the motion

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §§2.8.2-2.9: energy and angular-momentum level curves of the free rigid body and Euler's equations
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.4: free-rotation stability about the extreme and intermediate principal axes

items.title: Instability of spin about the intermediate principal axis of the torque-free top
items.statement: Let $I_1<I_2<I_3$ be positive reals, let $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear map with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ on the standard orthonormal basis, and consider the torque-free Euler system $l'=F(l)$, $F(l)=l\times(I^{-1}l)$, on $U=\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]], [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]). Let $L\ne0$. Then $l_0:=Le_2$ is an equilibrium of $F$ and is **not Lyapunov stable**: with $$\varepsilon_0:=\frac{|L|}{2},\qquad a:=\sqrt{\frac{1/I_1-1/I_2}{1/I_2-1/I_3}}>0,\qquad c_0:=a\Bigl(\frac1{I_2}-\frac1{I_3}\Bigr)\frac{\sqrt3}{2}|L|>0,$$ for every $\delta>0$ there is a solution $l$ with $\lVert l(0)-l_0\rVert_2<\delta$ and some $t\ge0$ with $\lVert l(t)-l_0\rVert_2\ge\varepsilon_0$; Moreover, with $\delta_0:=|L|/(2\sqrt{1+a^2})$, the escape can be arranged at a time $t\le c_0^{-1}\log(\delta_0/\eta)$ where $\eta=l_1(0)>0$ may be chosen as small as desired.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.4.3, Eqs. (3.40)-(3.45), printed pp. 57-58: explicit small perturbation of intermediate-axis spin, the invariant relation between the perturbations, and exponential growth
G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §§2.8.2-2.9: intermediate-axis behaviour on the angular-momentum level curves
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.4: instability of rotation about the intermediate principal axis

items.title: Linearization of the torque-free Euler system at a principal-axis spin, and the oscillatory/exponential dichotomy
items.statement:
Let $I_1,I_2,I_3>0$ be pairwise distinct, let $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the linear map with $Ie_j=I_je_j$ on the standard orthonormal basis, and let
$$F(\omega):=-I^{-1}\bigl(\omega\times I\omega\bigr),\qquad \omega\in\mathbb R^3,$$
be the torque-free Euler field in angular-velocity variables ([[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]]). Let $\Omega\ne0$. Then:

1. $F(\Omega e_3)=0$, and for every $\delta\in\mathbb R^3$ $$F(\Omega e_3+\delta)=A\delta+R(\delta),\qquad (A\delta)_1=\frac{\Omega(I_2-I_3)}{I_1}\delta_2,\quad (A\delta)_2=\frac{\Omega(I_3-I_1)}{I_2}\delta_1,\quad (A\delta)_3=0,$$ where $\lVert R(\delta)\rVert_2\le C\lVert\delta\rVert_2^2$ for the explicit constant $C:=\lVert I^{-1}\rVert_F\lVert I\rVert_F$ and $\lVert M\rVert_F:=\bigl(\sum_{j,k}M_{jk}^2\bigr)^{1/2}$; consequently $A$ is the total derivative of $F$ at $\Omega e_3$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]).
2. Every solution of the linear system $\delta'=A\delta$ on $\mathbb R$ has $\delta_3$ constant, and with $$\lambda:=\frac{\Omega^2(I_2-I_3)(I_3-I_1)}{I_1I_2}\ne0$$ the pair $(\delta_1,\delta_2)$ is determined by its initial value as follows:
   - if $\lambda<0$, then with $\kappa:=\sqrt{-\lambda}>0$, $$\delta_1(t)=\delta_1(0)\cos(\kappa t)+\frac{\Omega(I_2-I_3)}{I_1\kappa}\delta_2(0)\sin(\kappa t),\qquad \delta_2(t)=\delta_2(0)\cos(\kappa t)+\frac{\Omega(I_3-I_1)}{I_2\kappa}\delta_1(0)\sin(\kappa t),$$ and every solution is bounded on $[0,\infty)$;
   - if $\lambda>0$, then the same two formulas hold with $\cosh$ and $\sinh$ in place of $\cos$ and $\sin$ and $\kappa:=\sqrt\lambda$, the system has unbounded solutions (for instance $\delta_2(0)=0$, $\delta_1(0)\ne0$), and if $\delta_1(0)+\frac{\Omega(I_2-I_3)}{I_1\kappa}\delta_2(0)\ne0$ then $\lVert\delta(t)\rVert_2\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$.
3. Hence the linearization at the spin $\Omega e_3$ is oscillatory exactly when $(I_2-I_3)(I_3-I_1)<0$, i.e. when the third principal moment is a largest or a smallest moment, and it has exponentially growing solutions exactly when $\lambda>0$, i.e. when $I_3$ lies strictly between $I_1$ and $I_2$; in the latter case the zero solution of the linear system is not stable.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.4.3, Eqs. (3.41)-(3.45), printed pp. 57-58: perturbation of a principal-axis spin, the linearized equations and the sign criterion for oscillation versus exponential growth
G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §§2.8.2-2.9: linear behaviour near principal-axis spins

items.title: The coordinate rotation matrices $R_z(a)$ and $R_y(a)$: values in $SO(3)$, composition law, and derivatives
items.statement:
For $a\in\mathbb R$ define, in the standard basis of $\mathbb R^3$,
$$R_z(a):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos a&-\sin a&0\\ \sin a&\cos a&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(a):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos a&0&\sin a\\ 0&1&0\\ -\sin a&0&\cos a\end{pmatrix}\in M_3(\mathbb R).$$
Then:

1. $R_z(a)\in SO(3)$ and $R_y(a)\in SO(3)$ for every $a$ ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), $R_z(a)e_3=e_3$ and $R_y(a)e_2=e_2$, and $R_z(0)=R_y(0)=I_3$.
2. $R_z(a)R_z(b)=R_z(a+b)$ and $R_y(a)R_y(b)=R_y(a+b)$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R$.
3. For every differentiable $a:I\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-interval]]), the matrix-valued curves $t\mapsto R_z(a(t))$ and $t\mapsto R_y(a(t))$ are differentiable with $$(R_z\circ a)'=a'\,R_z(a)\,[e_3]_\times=a'\,[e_3]_\times R_z(a),\qquad (R_y\circ a)'=a'\,R_y(a)\,[e_2]_\times=a'\,[e_2]_\times R_y(a),$$ where $[e_3]_\times,[e_2]_\times$ are the cross-product matrices of [[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]].

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.5, Eqs. (3.53)-(3.58), printed pp. 62-65: the three ordered rotations and the Euler-angle parametrization of $SO(3)$
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.5, Eqs. (4.68)-(4.74): three successive rotations about coordinate axes, Euler angles and the angular-velocity components
G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §2.7 (Euler Angles): the rotation matrices about the coordinate axes and their products

items.title: The Euler-angle parametrization and the heavy symmetric top system
items.statement:
**Euler-angle parametrization.** Let $R_z,R_y$ be the coordinate rotation matrices of [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]]. The **Euler-angle parametrization** is the map
$$\Theta:\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad \Theta(\varphi,\theta,\psi):=R_z(\varphi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_z(\psi),$$
which is $SO(3)$-valued by [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]] and [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]. The numbers $(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ are the **Euler angles** and the open set $\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R$ is its **domain**; $\theta$ is restricted to the open interval $(0,\pi)$ so that $\sin\theta>0$. No injectivity and no chart or diffeomorphism property of $\Theta$ is asserted or used here, and no periodicity of the angles is imposed — the real parameters stand for themselves.

**Parameters.** Fix reals $A>0$, $C>0$, $m>0$, $d>0$ and $g>0$; they are mathematical parameters, not identified with any physical quantity in this item.

**The heavy-top function.** Write $q=(\varphi,\theta,\psi)$ for a point of the domain and $v=(\varphi',\theta',\psi')$ for a triple of reals. The **heavy-top function** is
$$L(q,v):=\tfrac12A\bigl(\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)+\tfrac12C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2-mgd\cos\theta,$$
using the sine and cosine of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]]. It is a composition of smooth functions of $(q,v)$ and is $C^\infty$ on the domain times $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); its relevant partial derivatives are, explicitly,
$$\partial_{\varphi'}L=A\varphi'\sin^2\theta+C\cos\theta\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \partial_\varphi L=0,$$
$$\partial_{\theta'}L=A\theta',\qquad \partial_\theta L=A\varphi'^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta,$$
$$\partial_{\psi'}L=C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr),\qquad \partial_\psi L=0.$$

**The heavy-top system.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points. A **heavy-top trajectory** for these parameters is a twice-differentiable curve $q=(\varphi,\theta,\psi):I\to\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R$ such that, with $q'=(\varphi',\theta',\psi')$ its derivative, the three second-order equations
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(A\varphi'\sin^2\theta+C\cos\theta\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\Bigr)=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}\bigl(A\theta'\bigr)=A\varphi'^2\sin\theta\cos\theta-C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\varphi'\sin\theta+mgd\sin\theta,$$
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)\Bigr)=0$$
hold on $I$, all functions being evaluated at $t$. These displayed equations are the definition of the system; they are written out so that no separate definition of a variational principle is needed. The first and third are the statements that $\partial_{\varphi'}L$ and $\partial_{\psi'}L$ are constant along the trajectory.

items.title: Angular velocity in Euler angles: $\omega_3=\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta$ and $\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2=\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta$
items.statement:
Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points, let $\varphi,\theta,\psi:J\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable with $\theta(J)\subseteq(0,\pi)$, and put
$$R(t):=\Theta\bigl(\varphi(t),\theta(t),\psi(t)\bigr)=R_z(\varphi(t))\,R_y(\theta(t))\,R_z(\psi(t)),$$
the Euler-angle parametrization of [[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]]. Then $R$ is a differentiable $SO(3)$-valued curve, and its **body angular velocity** $\omega:J\to\mathbb R^3$ in the sense of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]] (the unique vector with $R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times$) is, in the standard basis,
$$\omega=\bigl(-\varphi'\sin\theta\cos\psi+\theta'\sin\psi\bigr)e_1+\bigl(\varphi'\sin\theta\sin\psi+\theta'\cos\psi\bigr)e_2+\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)e_3,$$
all functions evaluated at $t$. Consequently
$$\omega_3=\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta,\qquad \omega_1^2+\omega_2^2=\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta,\qquad \lVert\omega\rVert_2^2=\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta+\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2.$$
Moreover, if $A,C>0$ and $I:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the linear map with $Ie_1=Ae_1$, $Ie_2=Ae_2$, $Ie_3=Ce_3$, then $\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=A\bigl(\theta'^2+\varphi'^2\sin^2\theta\bigr)+C\bigl(\psi'+\varphi'\cos\theta\bigr)^2$.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.5.2, Eqs. (3.55)-(3.58), printed pp. 64-65: angular velocity in terms of Euler angles, with $\omega_3=\dot\psi+\dot\varphi\cos\theta$ and the squared transverse component
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.5, Eq. (4.74): principal-axis components of the instantaneous angular velocity in Euler angles

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §2.7 (Euler Angles) and §2.10, Eq. (2.86): the kinetic energy $\tfrac12A(\dot\theta^2+\dot\varphi^2\sin^2\theta)+\tfrac12C(\dot\psi+\dot\varphi\cos\theta)^2$

items.title: Finite point-mass inertia matrices computed and checked against the positivity criterion
items.statement:
Throughout, the ambient data are the Euclidean inner product and cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), and $\nu$ is a finite weighted sum of Dirac measures at distinct points $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\mathbb R^3$ with weights $c_1,\dots,c_n>0$ ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]), which is a mass distribution of total mass $m=\sum_kc_k$ in the sense of [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; let $I=I(\nu)$ be its inertia matrix. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only through the Borel measurability of the polynomial integrands, which is what makes the entries of $I$ finite real numbers ([[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]]). Three cases are computed and each is checked against the positivity criterion of [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] and the principal-axis corollary [[cor-cm-principal-axes-of-the-inertia-matrix]].

**(i) Two unit masses on the third axis.** $n=2$, $x_1=e_3$, $x_2=-e_3$, $c_1=c_2=1$: then $m=2$, $\mu(\nu)=e_3-e_3=0$, and $I=\mathrm{diag}(2,2,0)$.

**(ii) Three unit masses at an equilateral triangle in the plane $e_3=0$.** $n=3$, $c_k=1$ and $x_k=\cos(2\pi k/3)e_1+\sin(2\pi k/3)e_2$ for $k=0,1,2$: then $m=3$, $\mu(\nu)=0$ and $I=\mathrm{diag}(\tfrac32,\tfrac32,3)$.

**(iii) Two unit masses on the first axis.** $n=2$, $x_1=e_1$, $x_2=2e_1$, $c_1=c_2=1$: then $m=2$, $\mu(\nu)=3e_1\ne0$, and $I=\mathrm{diag}(0,5,5)$.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.2, Eqs. (3.19)-(3.23), printed pp. 50-52: inertia tensors of finite point-mass systems and of a rod, with the semidefiniteness criterion
G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), §§2.3-2.5: moments of inertia of discrete mass distributions and the principal moments

items.title: Finite checks of the torque-free spin results: stability certificates, an escape-time bound, and the linearized dichotomy
items.statement: Fix the diagonal inertia map with principal moments $(I_1,I_2,I_3)=(1,2,3)$ ([[cor-cm-principal-axes-of-the-inertia-matrix]]) and the torque-free Euler system $l'=l\times(I^{-1}l)$ of [[thm-cm-euler-equations-and-torque-free-invariants]] on $\mathbb R^3$. The three computations below check the certificates of [[thm-cm-stability-of-extreme-principal-axes]], the escape bound of [[thm-cm-instability-of-the-intermediate-axis]], and the linearized formulas of [[thm-cm-linearized-torque-free-euler-equations]] at explicit numerical data. All numbers are exact rationals or explicit square roots; no measurement or simulation is involved, and no claim about a physical top is made.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §§3.4.1-3.4.3, printed pp. 55-58: free-top invariants and the intermediate-axis stability criterion used in these arithmetic checks
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Ch. 4 §4.4: principal-axis rotation stability, checked numerically here

items.title: Finite checks of the Euler-angle parametrization, the angular-velocity formula and a steady precession of the heavy top
items.statement: All data are the exact ones of the heavy-top system of [[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]] with the parameter choice $A=C=m=d=g=1$, and the rotation matrices are those of [[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]]. Three computations are performed: the value of the Euler-angle parametrization at a specific triple, the body angular velocity of a specific motion through the formula of [[lem-cm-euler-angle-angular-velocity]] checked against the definition, and a constant-rate precession checked against every clause of [[thm-cm-heavy-top-reduction]]. No physical measurement is involved and no claim about a physical top is made.
